report:
**Conclusion:**
Evidence indicates that magnesium supplementation can improve symptoms of mild-to-moderate depression, though it is generally recommended as an adjunctive (complementary) support rather than a primary replacement for standard medical treatments.

**Key Evidence:**
- **Clinical Meta-Analyses:** A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials found that magnesium supplementation yielded a statistically significant reduction in depressive symptoms among adults (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/).
- **Randomized Trial Results:** Clinical trials, such as a prominent study evaluating daily magnesium chloride (~248 mg elemental magnesium), observed rapid, clinically meaningful improvements in depression and anxiety scores within two weeks (https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/magnesium-dosage).
- **Biological Mechanisms:** Magnesium regulates N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and the stress-response pathway in the brain. It also supports neurotransmitter balance, which can indirectly boost mood by easing anxiety and improving sleep quality (https://time.com/6258780/magnesium-glycinate-sleep-anxiety-tiktok/).
- **Study Limitations:** Many existing trials feature small sample sizes and short follow-up periods. Consequently, clinical guidelines suggest using magnesium as an integrative option alongside standard interventions, such as psychotherapy or prescribed medication, under healthcare supervision (https://www.webmd.com/depression/magnesium-for-depression).
